title: A 32K-window proxy that beat full context on long agent histories
content:
Like Johnny, your agent carries more than its head can hold — and keeps working for hours.
A transparent HTTP proxy that sits between a coding agent and a local model (llama.cpp's llama-server,
Strata, ds4-server, or any
OpenAI-compatible server). The agent keeps sending its whole,
unmodified history; the proxy decides what the model actually reads. Old material leaves the prompt but is never
summarized away: every message, tool call and output stays on disk, verbatim, and the model can pull any of it back.
It speaks OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages and OpenAI Responses. Python ≥ 3.10, standard library only.
Developed and benchmarked primarily with Strata, by Niko1221 and contributors. mnemonic-proxy is an independently maintained project that also supports llama-server, ds4-server and other OpenAI-compatible backends; saved engine state depends on what the backend supports (see Engines).
Project page: https://lastreload.github.io/mnemonic-proxy/
Measured on our hardware (single runs, see What we have not proven): a 3 h 15 min coding session on one 12 GB GPU with 448K tokens of history and at most 105K in the prompt (One session, measured); AgentLongBench in a 32K window, 86/100 right with the proxy vs 47 with an LLM summary and 69 with the full history in a larger window (benchmark); a 110K-token conversation resumed from disk in 1.4 s instead of ≈50 s (Saved state, measured).
The first time: install, watch it work with no model, check your engine, start.
python3 -m venv mnemonic-venv && . mnemonic-venv/bin/activate
pip install mnemonic-proxy
mnemonic-proxy demo      # 1 minute, no model: archive, masking, recall -> PASS
mnemonic-proxy check --upstream http://127.0.0.1:8095 --port 8096 --data ./data --config config.json
mnemonic-proxy --upstream http://127.0.0.1:8095 --port 8096 --data ./data --config config.json
check ends with READY (exit 0) or says, line by line, what to change; --live adds a real generation, a tool
call and a save/restore. --upstream is the engine's address. Then point the agent at the proxy (port 8096)
instead of the engine. The engine window must be at least 16K tokens, 32K or more recommended
(Requirements). Step by step with a small model on CPU: Quick start.
Your engine. Start it as below, copy the config from
examples/ and set slot_dir to the engine's
save folder:
The proxy reads the window from Strata, llama-server (n_ctx, per model in router mode), ds4-server (--ctx),
Ollama and LM Studio (the context of the loaded model, 0.3.8), and scales its thresholds to it, unless window is
written in the config (the two Strata examples set 131072: change it if Strata runs with another window). From any
other engine it cannot: window in the config is used as it is (131072 when missing), so write the engine's real
context there; config.openai-32k.json has the thresholds the proxy itself uses at 32K. Details per engine:
Engines.
Ollama and LM Studio (tested on Linux, small model, details in Tested combinations). Both
serve an OpenAI-compatible API (Ollama http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1, LM Studio http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1;
--upstream is the same address without /v1) and the proxy runs in base mode: masking, archive, recall, segment
switches, tool calls, streaming, /v1/messages and /v1/responses worked, no saved state. What to know:
- Give the engine a context of 32768 (at least 16384). With their defaults on our machine (Ollama 4096 on CPU;
LM Studio 8192) both answer HTTP 200 to longer prompts after dropping part of them, without telling the client:
Ollama drops the oldest messages, LM Studio keeps the beginning and the end and drops the middle.
Ollama: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 ollama serve; ollama ps shows the context in use (column CONTEXT).
LM Studio: lms load <model> --context-length 32768, then lms server start; lms ps shows it.
- The proxy reads that context (0.3.8): Ollama GET /api/ps (context_length of the loaded model: the context
it runs with, not the training context of POST /api/show), LM Studio GET /api/v0/models (loaded_context_length). It reads it again before every request (one cheap GET; a model that is not loaded is
loaded first with a 1-token request), so the window follows the engine and a prompt never goes over it. Below
16384 the proxy refuses to start; a window in the config bigger than the engine context also refuses the start
and fails check, with the command that fixes it. You can leave window out of the config.
- --tokenizer is still recommended (the model's tokenizer.json, pip install 'mnemonic-proxy[exact]').
Without it the proxy estimates chars/3.5, which was up to ~10% low on code with many digits; on generic engines
the estimate now gets a 15% margin by default (window_estimate_slack 0.15) and check warns. With 0.3.7 the
notes request at a segment switch was estimated at 31.3K tokens but was 33.4K real tokens and both engines cut it;
with 0.3.8 and no tokenizer it was 27.7K real tokens on Ollama and nothing was cut (numbers in Tested
combinations).
- A cut prompt is reported: when the engine says (usage.prompt_tokens) it read less than 0.8× what the proxy
counted, the journal gets engine_truncated and the log one warning per conversation; check --live sends a
prompt of 0.9× the window and fails with "engine context smaller than window" if it does not come back whole.
- Ollama ignores an integrated GPU by default and runs on the CPU (much slower); OLLAMA_IGPU_ENABLE=1 makes it use
it. With it, Ollama chose a default context of 262144 from the shared memory: set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH anyway.
Your agent. Turn off the agent's own auto-compaction, otherwise two context managers fight over the same history:
Your OS.
- Linux: the reference; the commands on this page, and all the measured sessions.
- Windows, native: PowerShell commands and a one-click examples\start-windows.bat in Platforms
(tested on the CI runner, not yet on a desktop). WSL 2: the Linux commands, with engine, proxy and slots all
inside WSL.
- macOS: not tested yet; follow the Linux commands (llama.cpp from Homebrew or built with Metal), see Platforms.
- Android (Termux): pkg install python git, then pip install git+https://github.com/lastreload/mnemonic-proxy;
tested in Waydroid (Android 13, x86_64) in front of an online API, not yet on an ARM phone, see
Platforms.
No summaries written by a model, no vector database required.
- Hide — mask, don't summarize. Old tool outputs and reasoning leave the prompt in stable blocks and become one-line receipts with an id. The prefix stays byte-identical between blocks, so the engine's KV cache keeps working.
- Recall — structured, exact. A recall tool searches the verbatim archive: first write of a file, its full
edit timeline, command → output, the reasoning behind an edit — every hit tagged with message number and segment.
The proxy runs these calls itself; the client never sees them, even when streaming.
- Segment — handoff notes. When even the masked window fills up, the model writes its own notes, the segment is
sealed and a fresh one starts. Pinned lines (!! or 📌) survive every switch; lines starting with 🗑 (or ~)
mark a message as disposable once answered.
- Save — engine state on disk. On engines that support it (llama-server, Strata with session files) the KV state is saved to disk: resuming after a pause, a restart or another client takes 1–3 s instead of a full re-read.
- Archive — deduplicated cold storage. Old state files are rebuilt bit-for-bit from content-addressed zstd blocks: −36% disk on our sessions, sha256-verified before every restore.
- Lean — tools on demand. Agents ship tens of thousands of tokens of tool definitions. The proxy keeps the core ones and loads the rest by name: 25.6K → 6.2K tokens on every request.
"In the courier business you don't read the payload. You carry it, and you give it back exactly as it was." — the design rule. Hidden content is never paraphrased; it is either in the prompt or retrievable verbatim.
- Engine window: at least 16K tokens (16384

report.summary: A lightweight proxy for coding agents masks old history instead of summarizing it, keeping 32K-window local models accurate across 448K-token sessions with verbatim recall.
report.background: Coding agents accumulate enormous histories — every tool call, file edit and stack trace — and long sessions routinely blow past a local model's context window. The standard fixes are lossy: an LLM writes a summary (which silently drops detail the agent later needs), or the history is chunked into a vector database and retrieved by similarity. Both trade exactness for space. Meanwhile llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio quietly truncate over-long prompts and still return HTTP 200, so agents fail in confusing ways. mnemonic-proxy takes a different position: the model's prompt is a working set, not the record. Old material leaves the window in stable, cache-friendly blocks but is never paraphrased — it stays on disk, byte-for-byte, and can be pulled back on demand. The project is independently maintained and grew out of benchmarking work on Strata, with support for any OpenAI-compatible backend.
key_points: Mask, don't summarize: expired tool outputs and reasoning collapse into one-line receipts with IDs, keeping the prompt prefix byte-identical between blocks so the engine's KV cache stays warm. Nothing hidden is ever rewritten — content is either in the prompt or retrievable verbatim from the archive.

A structured recall tool searches the on-disk archive by message number and segment: first write of a file, its full edit timeline, command-to-output pairs, and the reasoning behind an edit. The proxy executes these calls itself, so the client never sees them, even mid-stream.

Segment handoffs handle the truly long haul. When the masked window fills, the model writes its own notes, the segment is sealed and a fresh one starts; pinned lines survive every switch and messages marked disposable are dropped once answered.

The numbers: a 3h15m session on one 12GB GPU with 448K tokens of history and at most 105K in the prompt; 86/100 on AgentLongBench in a 32K window versus 47 for an LLM summary and 69 for full history in a larger window; a 110K-token conversation resumed in 1.4s instead of ~50s.

Operational guardrails: the proxy reads the real context length from Strata, llama-server, ds4-server, Ollama and LM Studio, refuses to start below 16K, and logs engine_truncated when a backend silently cuts a prompt. Tool definitions are also lazy-loaded, cutting 25.6K tokens to 6.2K per request.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a pointed counter-argument to the summarization-and-vector-DB orthodoxy: context management becomes an infrastructure concern rather than a model behavior, and it works with standard-library Python against any OpenAI-compatible server. For developers, it means long agent runs on consumer hardware — a 12GB GPU handling half a million tokens of history — without rewriting the agent, since the proxy is transparent and the agent keeps sending its full, unmodified history. The caveats matter: benchmarks are single runs, macOS is untested, saved KV state only works on some engines, and agents must disable their own auto-compaction or two managers fight over the same history. For regular users, the practical effect is coding assistants that stop forgetting the file they edited an hour ago.
report.tools: Start with mnemonic-proxy itself (pip install mnemonic-proxy; a one-minute `demo` runs with no model, and `check --live` validates against your engine). Pair it with llama.cpp's llama-server or Strata for saved KV state, and ds4-server, Ollama or LM Studio for base mode — for Ollama set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768, and for LM Studio use `lms load --context-length 32768`. Install the [exact] extra for real tokenizer counts. AgentLongBench is the benchmark to reproduce the 32K-window results.
